title: Lelantos: A Blockchain-based Anonymous Physical Delivery System
authors: AlTawy, R. et al.
venue: 2017 15th Annual Conference on Privacy, Security and Trust (PST), IEEE, pp. 15-24
actors: customer (anonymous), merchant, a set of n customer-chosen delivery companies (couriers), and the Lelantos web server that advertises/certifies merchants' and delivery companies' public keys
L3_who: client-side: the customer app (Appc) encrypts the drop-off address and per-hop route ciphertexts with the merchant's and each delivery company's registered public keys
L4_staged: yes: onion-routing/Crowds-style route. Each delivery company knows only the previous and next hop. The next-hop address stays masked until the customer uploads mask_i via Next, or she picks the package up herself by revealing a secret committed at contract creation. The pickup point is not known in advance.
notes: Page numbers are PDF page indices; printed pages are 15-24. L1: the customer's fresh pseudonym per delivery is an operational assumption (the user is expected to do it), while delivery companies are required to use new pseudonyms per contract. L2: payment is held in contract escrow and released per hop. The paper claims to 'deal with the anonymous payment' (p.10), but payment unlinkability relies on fresh pseudonyms and on the customer's transactions going 'through multiple mixes' outside the system, so it is not coded as a mixer. L3 is encrypted-partial because all physical addresses and route data are encrypted, but the product identifier pid and the price are sent to the contract in plaintext (p.6-7). infraPrivacy is corrected from 'other: Tor' to 'none' because only listed values are allowed. The customer app may optionally reach the Lelantos web server over Tor (p.4), which is user-side network anonymity, not an infrastructure guarantee of the system. Evaluation: only gas estimates in the Remix IDE; the network is unspecified and no testnet is named. Domain: e-commerce physical goods routed through several delivery companies, with customer pickup or drone last mile, coded parcel-last-mile. Bib: the altawy2017lelantos entry in references2.bib (and paper-blockchain/references.bib) has a malformed pages field 'pages={15--1509}'; the correct range is 15--24.

title: Smart Contracts based on Blockchain for Logistics Management
authors: Álvarez-Díaz, N. et al. (with Herrera-Joancomartí, J.; Caballero-Gil, P.)
venue: IML '17: International Conference on Internet of Things and Machine Learning, Liverpool, UK (ACM)
actors: Sender and recipient (in the case study the same airline passenger, as EOAs); the package/bag (also an EOA); intermediaries (airport control points that update package state); an 'Auth' registration EOA; a trusted external agent that encrypts data. No customer/establishment/courier triad.
L3_who: server-side: a trusted external agent encrypts users' private data (EC-ElGamal on secp256k1) before it is written to the User contract, and later hands it to intermediaries. Not end-to-end; the agent holds the encryption key pair (pkS, skS).
L4_staged: partial: the sender's and recipient's addresses stay encrypted on-chain, and the external agent requests them from Bob and Alice and passes them only to each middleman that handles the package. Disclosure is need-to-know through the agent, not tied to an on-chain commitment by the carrier.
notes: The bib entry smart2020logistics has wrong metadata (author 'Unknown', year 2020, journal 'Conference Paper'). The PDF is Álvarez-Díaz, Herrera-Joancomartí & Caballero-Gil, IML'17, ACM 2017, DOI 10.1145/3109761.3158384. The case study is airport luggage, generalised to a sender -> intermediaries -> recipient package model, so domain is other-delivery (arguably generic logistics, not last-mile). L1 is 'none' rather than pseudonymous-addresses because the User contract binds each EOA to public name/contact data and requires a legal ID (e.g. passport number), although the ID itself is encrypted. The paper also says 'the privacy and the authenticity of this system depends on the security ... of elliptic curve cryptography' (p.7). L3: only users' private data (fiscal address, identification) is encrypted. Package state updates, owner/recipient addresses and intermediary lists are plaintext on-chain. infraPrivacy 'none': the contract-level write authorization (authorize, msg.sender policies) protects integrity, not confidentiality. The paper itself says 'Any EOA, independently of if it is part of the logistics system, can use the contracts because they are publicly accessible' (p.7). The paper notes a private network could be effective for a national airport network (p.5), but the prototype targets public Ethereum. ElGamal's homomorphic property is mentioned only as future work. A KeyStore contract on Ropsten stores public keys. Signatures use ecrecover. Verifier: all quotes re-checked verbatim on the stated pages, and the full text was searched for reputation/rating/review/zero-knowledge/permissioned/TLS with no hits beyond those noted.

actors: Vendors (software/hardware manufacturers, resellers, integrators), system operators (receive and distribute components), system end-users (energy consumers), registrars, certifiers, standards organizations, auditors

notes: The bib entry pal2018cyber has wrong metadata ('Pal, Omer and others', 'IEEE International Conference on Big Data'). The PDF authors are Liang, Shetty, Tosh, Ji and Li, and the venue is SecureComm 2018 (Springer LNICST), DOI 10.1007/978-3-030-01704-0_3, pp. 43-62 (confirmed by the verifier on link.springer.com). The paper notes 'For privacy concerns, system users are not necessarily enrolled with the registrar' (p.11). The authors' previous ProvChain work on privacy is cited only as related work. p.3 claims blockchain 'ensures confidentiality' but gives no encryption mechanism, so L3 stays 'none'. infraPrivacy: the channel scheme is justified in the paper as 'maximizing the efficiency of transaction confirmation and validation' (p.15), but p.9 frames channels as the answer to the Data Access/privacy concern ('Some blockchain implementations, such as Hyperledger, support channel scheme [12] which provides an isolated communication method but this still adds to the risks of data leakage during channel participation.'), and p.15 says 'rule checker controls data access to authorized entities.'

title: Blockchain-Based Agri-Food Supply Chain: A Complete Solution
authors: Affaf Shahid et al. (with A. Almogren, N. Javaid, F. A. Al-Zahrani, M. Zuair, M. Alam)
venue: IEEE Access, vol. 8, pp. 69230-69243

title: Blockchain-Based Solution for Distribution and Delivery of COVID-19 Vaccines
authors: Ahmad Musamih et al. (with R. Jayaraman, K. Salah, H. R. Hasan, I. Yaqoob, Y. Al-Hammadi)
venue: IEEE Access, vol. 9, pp. 71372-71387
actors: Raw-material suppliers, manufacturer (deploys contract, registers distributors), distributors (couriers), IoT-enabled smart vaccine container (on-chain actor), freezer farms, refrigerated storage, vaccination centers, beneficiaries
L3_who: none (no encryption; non-critical data in cloud storage with hash on-chain, critical data and events in plaintext on-chain)
notes: 'Public permissioned mode' means public Ethereum with role permissions in the smart contract (Solidity modifiers). The limitations confirm the public chain: 'the public Ethereum blockchain uses Proof-of-Work (PoW) consensus algorithm' (p.15), and users must spend Ether. So chainDesign = public-permissionless at the chain layer and infraPrivacy = role-based-access-control at contract level. A private permissioned chain and Quorum private transactions appear only as future work: 'To further improve privacy, the Quorum platform can be used to ensure that transactions between entities can be only viewed by those entities and nobody else.' (p.15). Testing used Remix IDE ('a random Ethereum address in the testing network', p.9). Gas cost in USD was estimated with ETH Gas Station prices (139 Gwei, 1862 USD, p.12). The architecture names Infura for the smart container and DApp, but no deployment to a public network is reported. The contract stores the container contents, actor addresses and the receiving vaccination center in plaintext, and all actors can view on-chain logs, transactions and violations as well as the off-chain (cloud) data. No encryption is used anywhere. Bib discrepancy: antal2021vaccine lists author 'Antal, Claudia and others', but the DOI and title match Musamih et al., IEEE Access 2021. Also, badr2021contactless ('A Blockchain-based Contactless Delivery System for Addressing COVID-19 and Other Pandemics'), the entry just before tian2022errand in references2.bib (and likewise in new_bibtex_clean.bib and paper-blockchain/references.bib), carries the same DOI 10.1109/ACCESS.2021.3079197. That DOI is misattributed there. Page numbers are PDF pages 1-16 (journal pages 71372-71387). Verifier: all quotes verbatim; no field changed.

title: A Blockchain-based Contactless Delivery System for Addressing COVID-19 and Other Pandemics
authors: Mittal, P. et al.
venue: 2021 IEEE International Conference on Blockchain (Blockchain), pp. 382-387
actors: Service provider (restaurant or retail store; creates orders and uploads the courier's health status), delivery personnel, and customer. Hospitals and test centres are mentioned only as possible verifiers of test results.
L3_who: not applicable (nothing is encrypted; order, customer and courier details go on-chain, readable by all participants)
infraPrivacy: permissioned-access, role-based-access-control (Fabric access-control rules R1-R8 control writes; R1 lets ANY participant READ everything)
notes: VERIFIED: every quote was found verbatim on the stated PDF page. DOI and pages (382-387) were confirmed from the PDF footer. Bib metadata error: in all three .bib files, the key badr2021contactless has this paper's title but the wrong authors, venue and DOI (Badr et al., IEEE Access, 10.1109/ACCESS.2021.3079197). The real paper is Mittal, Walthall, Cui, Skjellum & Guin, 2021 IEEE International Conference on Blockchain, pp. 382-387, DOI 10.1109/Blockchain53845.2021.00060. L1: the only privacy measure is a static pseudonymous ID for the courier (e.g., an employee number) that the service provider can map back. It is neither a wallet address nor per-order, but pseudonymous-addresses is the closest level ('other: static employer-assigned pseudonym' would be an alternative). Customers are not pseudonymized: customer details go on-chain, and the order ID may contain the customer's last name. Every member must establish an identity in the system (p.3). The courier's location trace and medical status are stored on-chain and readable by every participant (R1). Domain: generic contactless delivery from retail stores and restaurants, with food delivery as the main usage example (Sec. III-C); food-delivery would also be defensible. Evaluation: a real Fabric network across three desktop machines (10 organizations, one channel, Raft), measuring latency and throughput. This is coded private-network rather than local-emulator because it is a multi-machine deployment, not a single-node development chain. Pages are PDF pages (PDF p.1 = proceedings p.382).

title: A Decentralized Marketplace for Collaborative Manufacturing
authors: Adrian Hofmann et al. (Hofmann, Freichel, Winkelmann)
venue: Twenty-Ninth European Conference on Information Systems (ECIS 2021), research paper
actors: Buyers of manufacturing capacity; sellers (manufacturers with machines); dark-pool matching nodes run by participants; an optional stablecoin issuer. There is no courier or delivery actor: finished goods are just 'shipped to the buyer'.
platform: unspecified (proposes ERC20 capacity tokens, a Zcash/Monero-style privacy value token, and a Republic Protocol-style MPC dark pool)
L3_who: client-side: the buyer encrypts the production information with the seller's public key (optional). Order price and volume are secret-shared across MPC dark-pool nodes.
zkp: yes (proposed only, not implemented): recommends a Zcash-style zk-SNARK value token, with Monero-style ring signatures as the alternative; order matching uses secure multiparty computation (dark pool), which is not a ZKP
notes: Page numbers are PDF page indices (PDF p.1 is a ResearchGate cover, so PDF p.N is printed p.N-1). The L1 quote begins at the bottom of PDF p.8 ('If suppliers') and continues on p.9. This is a conceptual design-science artifact evaluated only through interviews with 3 experts, with no prototype; the authors state it is 'not ready to be implemented in practical environments' (p.13). Every privacy feature is a recommendation, not a design detail: optional fresh addresses per sale, a Zcash/Monero-style value token (shielded pool, or ring signatures), optional encryption of production data with the counterparty's key, and MPC matching. ERC20 implies an EVM chain, but Ethereum is never named, so platform = unspecified. Domain fit is weak: it is a B2B manufacturing-capacity marketplace with no courier role. supply-chain-with-delivery is used because the paper places itself under 'supply network blockchains'; other-delivery is an alternative. L4: production details reach the seller only after the token swap. That parallels staged disclosure, but the recipient is the manufacturer, not a courier, so L4 = none. Public vs consortium deployment is left open (chainDesign unspecified). The consortium option is motivated by efficiency, cost and trusted membership against fraud, not privacy, so infraPrivacy = none. An escrow contract is only future work (p.12). The bib entry has no DOI (AIS eLibrary paper).

title: A Secure Proof of Delivery Scheme for Crowdsourced Last Mile Delivery Using Blockchain
authors: Vipul Malhotra
venue: M.Sc. thesis, School of Computer Science, University of Windsor (Electronic Theses and Dissertations 8605)
actors: Seller, buyer, a pool of crowdsourced carriers, and an arbitrator (trusted third party for off-chain disputes and reputation weights)
platform: Ethereum (Solidity smart contracts; Remix, Truffle, Ganache-cli, web3.js; RSA blind-signature package off-chain)
L3_who: not applicable (no encryption; the buyer's delivery location is a plaintext string argument emitted in a contract event)
infraPrivacy: role-based-access-control (smart-contract function modifiers restricting which address may call which function; no read privacy)
zkp: no (uses RSA blind signatures for buyer/proof-of-delivery verification, not ZKPs)
notes: Verifier re-read the relevant chapters and confirmed every field; all quotes appear verbatim on the stated PDF pages. Page numbers are PDF page indices (printed page = PDF page - 14, e.g., PDF p.47 = printed p.33). Table 3.4.1 (PDF p.68, checked on the rendered image) marks the proposed PoD system ✗ for ANONYMITY, while Lelantos (altawy2017lelantos) is ✓. The blind signatures let the seller sign a buyer-blinded token, so anyone holding it can collect the parcel. This is authentication and nominee pickup, not anonymity or anonymous rating. Carrier reputation is an on-chain score per carrier address (buyer and seller ratings weighted by the arbitrator) and drives carrier selection. Payments: the buyer deposits the item price in the contract. The appendix code (settle_payment) does seller.transfer(90*itemPrice/100) and transporter.transfer(10*itemPrice/100), a transparent escrow linking payer and payees. Appendix code (PDF p.98): delivery_attributes(bool custm_Delivery, string location) emits the location in plaintext in a DeliveryAttributes event. Inconsistency: the introduction (PDF p.18) speaks of 'an immutable permission-ed blockchain network', but the design chapter specifies public Ethereum with PoW, and the thesis followed the design chapter. Experiments ran 258 orders from a Bogotá online food-order dataset on Ganache. The gas tables (PDF p.79) show block gas limit 6721975, which is Ganache's default. Costs are estimated at 58 Gwei, $787.71 per delivery for the full flow. BIB PROBLEM (confirmed): malhotra2021secure is typed @phdthesis, but the title page says 'the Degree of Master of Science' (should be @mastersthesis).

title: Blockchain driven IoT based Delish2Go Decentralized Food Delivery Application
authors: K. Sasikala Rani et al. (with S. Vishali)
venue: 2021 International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Smart Systems (ICAIS), IEEE, pp. 1727-1732
actors: Customer, restaurant, delivery person/partner, raw-material supplier (updates food data), application administrator
platform: Ethereum (EVM/Solidity, ERC-20 token; network not specified)
L3_who: none (no encryption; delivery information stored on-chain)
notes: A short, low-detail paper whose design actively reduces privacy. Restaurant KYC is 'made transparent' (p.3), delivery partners' biometric KYC is stored on the blockchain, and a public explorer exposes the KYC and previous orders of restaurants and delivery partners. The user address goes through a 'blockchain based verification system' (p.3). It recognises the courier-privacy problem ('you likewise can't uncover each data of the conveyance young men as that would be bargaining their private data', p.2) but proposes nothing for it. Platform 'Ethereum' is inferred from the ERC-20 DelishToken code, 'pragma solidity ^0.6.0' and a Truffle-style Migrations contract (p.3-4), plus the EVM discussion (p.2). The paper never names the network, and 'Consensus Blockchain network' is unexplained, so chainDesign = unspecified. Evaluation = none: the prototype front-end ran on localhost (the screenshot address bar on p.5 reads 'localhost:3000/restaurant/register', checked by zooming into the rendered page), and the Migrations contract plus Ganache and MetaMask in the references suggest a local chain, but this is not stated. Fiat payments are also accepted. Despite the title, no IoT component is described. L1 = none rather than pseudonymous-addresses because restaurant and courier identities are deliberately bound to public KYC. Customer wallet identity is not described. Verifier: all quotes verbatim; no field changed.

title: Enacting the Last Mile: Experiences of Smart Contracts in Courier Deliveries
authors: Tallyn, E. et al.
venue: CHI '21: ACM CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems, 14 pages
actors: sender, courier (professional bicycle couriers from the Zedify company), recipient (university receptionists), courier-company manager; smart lock-boxes, unstaffed hubs, a smartphone app and the GeoServer
L3_who: n/a (no encryption described)
notes: An HCI user-enactment study (6 couriers, 4 receptionists, 1 manager) that uses a new iteration of the GeoPact assembly. Page numbers are PDF page indices. This paper says nothing about encryption, while its 2020 predecessor (tallyn2020geopact) has one sentence on beacon-data encryption. That is why the two GeoPact records differ on L3.

title: Security Enhancement in Smart Logistics with Blockchain Technology: A Home Delivery Use Case
authors: Tirajet Chukleang et al.
venue: Informatics (MDPI) 2022, 9(3), 70
actors: customer (client); producer (restaurant); distributor (rider); food delivery platform (off-chain app + RDBMS)
L3_who: n/a
notes: Domain: the use case and the 20-restaurant/20-rider experiment are food delivery; Section 2.1 also frames parcel delivery as the example, so parcel-last-mile is the alternative. Evaluation: Ganache 2.5.4 on a laptop, and the authors call it 'the blockchain simulation named "Ganache"' (p.15). L3 = none: Algorithm 1 stores '<Ψo, τ, desc, status>' on-chain, and desc is 'the description of the product or parcel and its status, such as the menu and drink items' (p.10), 'represented in JSON format' (p.12). title: Self-Sovereign Identity for Privacy-Preserving Shipping Verification System
authors: Andrea De Salve et al.
venue: 5th International Conference on Blockchain Technology and Applications (ICBTA 2022), ACM, pp. 147-157
actors: customer; marketplace (seller, credential issuer/endorser); shipping deliverer (courier); mailbox/parcel locker (verifier); steward (Indy node operator)
L1_identity: other (SSI: customer and mailbox use per-relationship Anonym/private DIDs over DID-to-DID channels; only the marketplace and steward DIDs are public; Indy anonymous credentials)
L3_who: client-side end-to-end: Indy agents/wallets of each actor; order and credential data travel over pairwise DID-to-DID secure channels and only public DIDs, schemas and credential definitions go on the ledger
zkp: yes: Hyperledger Indy AnonCreds (Camenisch-Lysyanskaya signature credential proofs with selective attribute disclosure); ZK predicates are described in the background
notes: Verifier: quotes for all kept fields re-checked verbatim on the stated pages. Two changes: L4 partial→none and infraPrivacy→none (see corrections). Evaluation runs on two testbeds: a 4-node local Indy pool 'on a local virtual network' (p.7) and Sovrin BuilderNet, a public developer test network of a permissioned ledger. public-testnet is chosen for BuilderNet, whose schema/credential-definition transactions are publicly viewable on indyscan. L3 = encrypted-full because no order content is written on-ledger: orders and credentials are exchanged agent-to-agent and stored in wallets. Each actor's DID comes with keys 'that will be used for signing and for encryption' (p.7), and 'messages exchanged are encrypted' appears in the general SSI introduction (p.2); the scheme itself is not detailed. Address protection comes from the parcel-locker design, not from staged disclosure: customers select a mailbox instead of giving a home address, and the deliverer's Shipment Parcel credential carries no customer DID or address (the Customer Shipping credential with didDest and itemName goes only to the customer). This is worth citing as an alternative to staged disclosure, but it does not count as L4. The deliverer's own DID handling is not described as anonymous (it only 'Create DID'). ZK comes from the Indy AnonCreds stack, not from a design contribution. The proof requests shown reveal attributes (shipmentId, nonce, availability), and predicate use is not demonstrated; zkp=yes rests on AnonCreds CL-signature proofs being ZK proofs of knowledge. Indy is a 'public permissioned' ledger (public read, permissioned write); chainDesign permissioned-consortium-private reflects the write side.

title: PackChain: Toward a Blockchain-based Management Platform for Last-mile Delivery
authors: El Moudaa, S. et al.
venue: 2022 International Wireless Communications and Mobile Computing (IWCMC), IEEE, pp. 919-924
actors: client (requester) and carrier (crowdsourced worker); the smart contract and SWARM decentralized storage
L3_who: none: no encryption. The client uploads plaintext package data (start/end positions, dimensions, weight) to SWARM; its content hash goes on-chain.
notes: Page numbers are PDF page indices. chainDesign: the paper never says 'public' explicitly. public-permissionless is inferred from 'the Ethereum blockchain' plus open registration with self-created Ethereum addresses 'without the need for any external entity'. It was tested only on Ganache. The paper lists 'Unique Identifiers are stored on chain publicly, affecting the privacy' (p.1) as a limitation of prior work, yet PackChain itself stores client/carrier addresses and public keys on-chain. L2: a direct prepayment to the carrier plus a deposit escrowed until a signature-based proof of delivery; payer and payee addresses are linked on-chain. L3: SWARM content is unencrypted and addressed by the on-chain hash, so anyone with the hash can retrieve the pickup/delivery positions. Verifier: the full text was re-read and all quotes confirmed verbatim on the stated pages; no field changed.

title: FoodChain: A Food Delivery Platform Based on Blockchain for Keeping Data Privacy
authors: Folha, R. et al.
venue: DASFAA 2022, LNCS 13247, Springer, pp. 500-504 (demo paper)
actors: customer, establishment/restaurant, courier; plus a Node.js API with a PostgreSQL database for public restaurant/menu data
L3_who: client-side end-to-end: the customer encrypts with the restaurant's, the courier's and her own public keys (MetaMask 'manages the encryption operations')
L4_staged: yes: the restaurant gets only the encrypted item list, without the customer's name or address. After a courier accepts the delivery, the customer encrypts name, address and items with the courier's public key.
notes: This is the authors' own earlier conference/demo version of the system. Page numbers are PDF page indices; printed pages are 500-504. L3 is coded encrypted-full because the items, the customer's name and the delivery address are all encrypted. Order metadata stays in plaintext on-chain: status, timestamps, the customer/restaurant/courier addresses and the delivery price ("mostly non-sensitive and stored as plain text", p.3). The encryption scheme is not named, only 'asymmetric encryption' via MetaMask. L2: the paper never describes how payment is made, so it is coded none; no-payment-on-chain is a defensible alternative. Verifier: every quote was checked verbatim against the PDF text, and the full text was re-read; no field changed. The bibKey matches the title in references2.bib (line 1451) and paper-blockchain/references.bib.

title: Towards a Novel Business Process Model for Food Delivery Services Using Blockchain Technology
authors: Folha, R. et al. (with Times, V.C.; Carvalho, A.; Araújo, A.; Viana, F.; Couto, H.)
venue: AMCIS 2022 Proceedings (Americas Conference on Information Systems, SIG Green), paper 5, AIS
actors: Customer, restaurant (establishment), delivery worker (courier); no platform intermediary
platform: Ethereum (Solidity contracts Chain, Order, View, Interact, Storage; MetaMask DApps)
L3_who: client-side end-to-end: the customer encrypts order details with the restaurant's public key, and personal data plus items with the delivery worker's public key. Only the holder of the matching private key decrypts. Keys are managed in the MetaMask wallets.
L4_staged: yes: the courier first accepts the job by publishing a public key to the Storage contract (and posts a deposit, held in escrow). Only then does the customer encrypt name, phone, address and items to that key and post them to Storage for the courier to decrypt.
notes: This is the authors' own earlier AMCIS 2022 paper (FoodChain line, distinct from DASFAA 2022 folha2022foodchain). No DOI. AISeL URL: https://aisel.aisnet.org/amcis2022/sig_green/sig_green/5. Page numbers are PDF pages: the AISeL file has 2 cover pages, so PDF p.N = printed p.N-2. chainDesign: the prototype runs on public Ethereum (Ropsten), but the paper argues mainnet is too expensive (about US$159 per order at 5,253,369 gas) and recommends a permissioned consortium network ('Instead, a permissioned network should be created to reduce costs', p.9). That recommendation is for cost, not privacy, so infraPrivacy is 'none'. Evaluation: contracts were on Ropsten. Separately, throughput (309 tx/s) was measured with the DLPS writeMuchData benchmark on a 10-node permissioned Ethereum network on AWS (private-network), but that is a generic benchmark, not the FoodChain contracts. L3: the design text (p.6) and the Privacy section (p.11) say order details are encrypted. However, the Demonstration section (p.8) says the Order contract stores 'the ordered items together with prices, the delivery fee, and information about all deposited values' without saying they are encrypted, and deposits and delivery fee are necessarily visible as escrowed ETH. The verifier also checked the April 2022 repository snapshot (commit 30d9af7): Order.sol keeps `total` and `deliveryPrice` as plaintext uint256 and `items` as a string. encrypted-full reflects the stated design; if the thesis wants the strictest reading, encrypted-partial would be defensible, and this ambiguity remains. L1: parties are plain MetaMask addresses, and the same address is reused across orders. p.6 also says accepted-job information including 'the driver’s info' is stored on-chain (contents unspecified). The paper claims 'stakeholders’ true identities are only disclosed to the appropriate parties' (p.4).

title: Decentralized Procurement Mechanisms for Efficient Logistics Services Mapping - a Design Science Research Approach
authors: Henry, T. et al. (Tiphaine Henry, Roman Beck, Nassim Laga, Walid Gaaloul, Shenle Pan)
venue: Proceedings of the 55th Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences (HICSS-55), pp. 5050-5059

(p.6), which supports public-reputation.

title: Managing Scores of Crowdsourcing Workers Using Blockchain
authors: Konomi, K. and Kamiyama, N.
